                                                     Take A Leap Into Hyperspace
  From: Eleanor White <eleanor.nul>
  Date: Fri, 06 Jan 2006 16:36:45 -0500
  Fwd Date: Sat, 07 Jan 2006 08:16:40 -0500
  Subject: Take A Leap Into Hyperspace


  Source: NewScientist.com News Service
  http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg18925331.200
  05 January 2006

  Take A Leap Into Hyperspace
  Haiko Lietz
  Every year, the American Institute of Aeronautics and
  Astronautics awards prizes for the best papers presented at its
  annual conference. Last year's winner in the nuclear and future
  flight category went to a paper calling for experimental tests
  of an astonishing new type of engine. According to the paper,
  this hyperdrive motor would propel a craft through another
  dimension at enormous speeds. It could leave Earth at lunchtime
  and get to the moon in time for dinner. There's just one catch:
  the idea relies on an obscure and largely unrecognised kind of
  physics. Can they possibly be serious?
  The AIAA is certainly not embarrassed. What's more, the US
  military has begun to cast its eyes over the hyperdrive concept,
  and a space propulsion researcher at the US Department of
  Energy's Sandia National Laboratories has said he would be
  interested in putting the idea to the test. And despite the
  bafflement of most physicists at the theory that supposedly
  underpins it, Pavlos Mikellides, an aerospace engineer at the
  Arizona State University in Tempe who reviewed the winning
  paper, stands by the committee's choice. "Even though such
  features have been explored before, this particular approach is
  quite unique," he says.
  Unique it certainly is. If the experiment gets the go-ahead and
  works, it could reveal new interactions between the fundamental
  forces of nature that would change the future of space travel.
  Forget spending six months or more holed up in a rocket on the
  way to Mars, a round trip on the hyperdrive could take as little
  as 5 hours. All our worries about astronauts' muscles wasting
  away or their DNA being irreparably damaged by cosmic radiation
  would disappear overnight. What's more the device would put
  travel to the stars within reach for the first time. But can the
  hyperdrive really get off the ground?
  The answer to that question hinges on the work of a little-known
  German physicist. Burkhard Heim began to explore the hyperdrive
  propulsion concept in the 1950s as a spin-off from his attempts
  to heal the biggest divide in physics: the rift between quantum
  mechanics and Einstein's general theory of relativity.
  Quantum theory describes the realm of the very small - atoms,
  electrons and elementary particles - while general relativity
  deals with gravity. The two theories are immensely successful in
  their separate spheres. The clash arises when it comes to
  describing the basic structure of space. In general relativity,
  space-time is an active, malleable fabric. It has four
  dimensions - three of space and one of time - that deform when
  masses are placed in them. In Einstein's formulation, the force


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m07-002.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:32]
Take A Leap Into Hyperspace

  of gravity is a result of the deformation of these dimensions.
  Quantum theory, on the other hand, demands that space is a fixed
  and passive stage, something simply there for particles to exist
  on. It also suggests that space itself must somehow be made up
  of discrete, quantum elements.
  In the early 1950s, Heim began to rewrite the equations of
  general relativity in a quantum framework. He drew on Einstein's
  idea that the gravitational force emerges from the dimensions of
  space and time, but suggested that all fundamental forces,
  including electromagnetism, might emerge from a new, different
  set of dimensions. Originally he had four extra dimensions, but
  he discarded two of them believing that they did not produce any
  forces, and settled for adding a new two-dimensional "sub-space"
  onto Einstein's four-dimensional space-time.
  In Heim's six-dimensional world, the forces of gravity and
  electromagnetism are coupled together. Even in our familiar
  four-dimensional world, we can see a link between the two forces
  through the behaviour of fundamental particles such as the
  electron. An electron has both mass and charge. When an electron
  falls under the pull of gravity its moving electric charge
  creates a magnetic field. And if you use an electromagnetic
  field to accelerate an electron you move the gravitational field
  associated with its mass. But in the four dimensions we know,
  you cannot change the strength of gravity simply by cranking up
  the electromagnetic field.
  In Heim's view of space and time, this limitation disappears. He
  claimed it is possible to convert electromagnetic energy into
  gravitational and back again, and speculated that a rotating
  magnetic field could reduce the influence of gravity on a
  spacecraft enough for it to take off.
  When he presented his idea in public in 1957, he became an
  instant celebrity. Wernher von Braun, the German engineer who at
  the time was leading the Saturn rocket programme that later
  launched astronauts to the moon, approached Heim about his work
  and asked whether the expensive Saturn rockets were worthwhile.
  And in a letter in 1964, the German relativity theorist Pascual
  Jordan, who had worked with the distinguished physicists Max
  Born and Werner Heisenberg and was a member of the Nobel
  committee, told Heim that his plan was so important "that its
  successful experimental treatment would without doubt make the
  researcher a candidate for the Nobel prize".
  But all this attention only led Heim to retreat from the public
  eye. This was partly because of his severe multiple
  disabilities, caused by a lab accident when he was still in his
  teens. But Heim was also reluctant to disclose his theory
  without an experiment to prove it. He never learned English
  because he did not want his work to leave the country. As a
  result, very few people knew about his work and no one came up
  with the necessary research funding. In 1958 the aerospace
  company Bolkow did offer some money, but not enough to do the
  proposed experiment.
  While Heim waited for more money to come in, the company's
  director, Ludwig Bolkow, encouraged him to develop his theory
  further. Heim took his advice, and one of the results was a
  theorem that led to a series of formulae for calculating the
  masses of the fundamental particles - something conventional
  theories have conspicuously failed to achieve. He outlined this
  work in 1977 in the Max Planck Institute's journal Zeitschrift
  f=FCr Naturforschung, his only peer-reviewed paper. In an abstruse
  way that few physicists even claim to understand, the formulae
  work out a particle's mass starting from physical
  characteristics, such as its charge and angular momentum.
  Yet the theorem has proved surprisingly powerful. The standard
  model of physics, which is generally accepted as the best
  available theory of elementary particles, is incapable of
  predicting a particle's mass. Even the accepted means of
  estimating mass theoretically, known as lattice quantum
  chromodynamics, only gets to between 1 and 10 per cent of the
  experimental values. Gravity reduction
  But in 1982, when researchers at the German Electron Synchrotron
  (DESY) in Hamburg implemented Heim's mass theorem in a computer
  program, it predicted masses of fundamental particles that
  matched the measured values to within the accuracy of


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m07-002.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:32]
Take A Leap Into Hyperspace

  experimental error. If they are let down by anything, it is the
  precision to which we know the values of the fundamental
  constants. Two years after Heim's death in 2001, his long-term
  collaborator Illobrand von Ludwiger calculated the mass formula
  using a more accurate gravitational constant. "The masses came
  out even more precise," he says.
  After publishing the mass formulae, Heim never really looked at
  hyperspace propulsion again. Instead, in response to requests
  for more information about the theory behind the mass
  predictions, he spent all his time detailing his ideas in three
  books published in German. It was only in 1980, when the first
  of his books came to the attention of a retired Austrian patent
  officer called Walter Droscher, that the hyperspace propulsion
  idea came back to life. Droscher looked again at Heim's ideas
  and produced an "extended" version, resurrecting the dimensions
  that Heim originally discarded. The result is "Heim-Droscher
  space", a mathematical description of an eight-dimensional
  universe.
  =46rom this, Droscher claims, you can derive the four forces
  known in physics: the gravitational and electromagnetic forces,
  and the strong and weak nuclear forces. But there's more to it
  than that. "If Heim's picture is to make sense," Droscher says,
  "we are forced to postulate two more fundamental forces." These
  are, Droscher claims, related to the familiar gravitational
  force: one is a repulsive anti-gravity similar to the dark
  energy that appears to be causing the universe's expansion to
  accelerate. And the other might be used to accelerate a
  spacecraft without any rocket fuel.
  This force is a result of the interaction of Heim's fifth and
  sixth dimensions and the extra dimensions that Droscher
  introduced. It produces pairs of "gravitophotons", particles
  that mediate the interconversion of electromagnetic and
  gravitational energy. Droscher teamed up with Jochem H=E4user, a
  physicist and professor of computer science at the University of
  Applied Sciences in Salzgitter, Germany, to turn the theoretical
  framework into a proposal for an experimental test. The paper
  they produced, "Guidelines for a space propulsion device based
  on Heim's quantum theory", is what won the AIAA's award last
  year.
  Claims of the possibility of "gravity reduction" or "anti-
  gravity" induced by magnetic fields have been investigated by
  NASA before (New Scientist, 12 January 2002, p 24). But this
  one, Droscher insists, is different. "Our theory is not about
  anti-gravity. It's about completely new fields with new
  properties," he says. And he and H=E4user have suggested an
  experiment to prove it.
  This will require a huge rotating ring placed above a
  superconducting coil to create an intense magnetic field. With a
  large enough current in the coil, and a large enough magnetic
  field, Droscher claims the electromagnetic force can reduce the
  gravitational pull on the ring to the point where it floats
  free. Droscher and H=E4user say that to completely counter Earth's
  pull on a 150-tonne spacecraft a magnetic field of around 25
  tesla would be needed. While that's 500,000 times the strength
  of Earth's magnetic field, pulsed magnets briefly reach field
  strengths up to 80 tesla. And Droscher and H=E4user go further.
  With a faster-spinning ring and an even stronger magnetic field,
  gravitophotons would interact with conventional gravity to
  produce a repulsive anti-gravity force, they suggest.
  Droscher is hazy about the details, but he suggests that a
  spacecraft fitted with a coil and ring could be propelled into a
  multidimensional hyperspace. Here the constants of nature could
  be different, and even the speed of light could be several times
  faster than we experience. If this happens, it would be possible
  to reach Mars in less than 3 hours and a star 11 light years
  away in only 80 days, Droscher and H=E4user say.
  So is this all fanciful nonsense, or a revolution in the making?
  The majority of physicists have never heard of Heim theory, and
  most of those contacted by New Scientist said they couldn't make
  sense of Droscher and H=E4user's description of the theory behind
  their proposed experiment. Following Heim theory is hard work
  even without Droscher's extension, says Markus Possel, a
  theoretical physicist at the Max Planck Institute for
  Gravitational Physics in Potsdam, Germany. Several years ago,


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m07-002.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:32]
Take A Leap Into Hyperspace

  while an undergraduate at the University of Hamburg, he took a
  careful look at Heim theory. He says he finds it "largely
  incomprehensible", and difficult to tie in with today's physics.
  "What is needed is a step-by-step introduction, beginning at
  modern physical concepts," he says.
  The general consensus seems to be that Droscher and H=E4user's
  theory is incomplete at best, and certainly extremely difficult
  to follow. And it has not passed any normal form of peer review,
  a fact that surprised the AIAA prize reviewers when they made
  their decision. "It seemed to be quite developed and ready for
  such publication," Mikellides told New Scientist.
  At the moment, the main reason for taking the proposal seriously
  must be Heim theory's uncannily successful prediction of
  particle masses. Maybe, just maybe, Heim theory really does have
  something to contribute to modern physics. "As far as I
  understand it, Heim theory is ingenious," says Hans Theodor
  Auerbach, a theoretical physicist at the Swiss Federal Institute
  of Technology in Zurich who worked with Heim. "I think that
  physics will take this direction in the future."
  It may be a long while before we find out if he's right. In its
  present design, Droscher and H=E4user's experiment requires a
  magnetic coil several metres in diameter capable of sustaining
  an enormous current density. Most engineers say that this is not
  feasible with existing materials and technology, but Roger
  Lenard, a space propulsion researcher at Sandia National
  Laboratories in New Mexico thinks it might just be possible.
  Sandia runs an X-ray generator known as the Z machine which
  "could probably generate the necessary field intensities and
  gradients".
  For now, though, Lenard considers the theory too shaky to
  justify the use of the Z machine. "I would be very interested in
  getting Sandia interested if we could get a more perspicacious
  introduction to the mathematics behind the proposed experiment,"
  he says. "Even if the results are negative, that, in my mind, is
  a successful experiment."
  =46rom issue 2533 of New Scientist magazine, 05 January 2006,
  page 24

  Who was Burkhard Heim?
  Burkhard Heim had a remarkable life. Born in 1925 in Potsdam,
  Germany, he decided at the age of 6 that he wanted to become a
  rocket scientist. He disguised his designs in code so that no
  one could discover his secret. And in the cellar of his parents'
  house, he experimented with high explosives. But this was to
  lead to disaster.
  Towards the end of the second world war, he worked as an
  explosives developer, and an accident in 1944 in which a device
  exploded in his hands left him permanently disabled. He lost
  both his forearms, along with 90 per cent of his hearing and
  eyesight.
  After the war, he attended university in Gottingen to study
  physics. The idea of propelling a spacecraft using quantum
  mechanics rather than rocket fuel led him to study general
  relativity and quantum mechanics. It took an enormous effort.
  =46rom 1948, his father and wife replaced his senses, spending
  hours reading papers and transcribing his calculations onto
  paper. And he developed a photographic memory.
  Supporters of Heim theory claim that it is a panacea for the
  troubles in modern physics. They say it unites quantum mechanics
  and general relativity, can predict the masses of the building
  blocks of matter from first principles, and can even explain the
  state of the universe 13.7 billion years ago.

  On Fri, 6 Jan 2006, Leonard R. Cleavelin wrote:
  >Welcome to Mars express: only a three hour trip
  >http://news.scotsman.com/scitech.cfm?id=16902006
  >AN EXTRAORDINARY "hyperspace" engine that could make
  >interstellar space travel a reality by flying into other
  >dimensions is being investigated by the United States
  >government.
  I'm afraid that's science reporting pretty much at its worst,
  and I'm very much disappointed with New Scientist for the way
  this was presented. (Or did I have too high an opinion of that
  magazine to start with?)
  Fact is that the man they're talking about, Burkhard Heim, who
  worked out the theory in question as his personal take on the
  problem of quantum gravity, never managed to write it down in a
  way comprehensible to the relevant experts - the people working
  in elementary particle physics, general relativity and so on.
  (And, as such, he never managed to publish his theory in the
  regular way in a research journal.)
  A long time ago, I tried to read the books he eventually
  published on his theory, but I gave up pretty soon. In the
  opening chapters, it seemed that he got even ordinary Newtonian
  physics and basic special relativity wrong, and after that, the
  exposition proceeded in logical jumps that I couldn't follow at
  all.
  [The reason I came across Heim's books in the first place is, by
  the way, very much on topic for this list: Pretty much the only
  people who tried to come to terms with what Heim was doing were
  some gentlemen from MUFON-CES, the Central European Section of
  the Mutual UFO Network, and they were interested in how, using
  Heim's theory, one might be able to explain certain UFO
  manifestations (energy coming from higher dimensions?). Those
  also appear to be the prime movers behind what little PR there
  is for the theory, for instance the website www.heim-theory.com,
  and they're quoted in the New Scientist article as well.]
  So if the kind people from New Scientist had behaved in a
  responsible manner, they a) either wouldn't have given this
  theory any publicity at all, or b) they would have written their
  article in a way that makes the following crucial fact clear to
  any reader: This theory hasn't even passed the first hurdle for
  scientific theories. It has never been set out in a form that is
  comprehensible to the relevant subsection of the scientific
  community, and thus it hasn't been subjected to any of the
  critical scrutiny and discussion that are part of the scientific
  quality assurance process. Consequently, it fails even the most
  basic requirements that any scientific theory must meet before
  it can be taken seriously.

  The Scotsman, by the way, manages to present matters even less
  accurately than New Scientist. Take this paragraph:
  "The US air force has expressed an interest in the idea and
  scientists working for the American Department of Energy - which
  has a device known as the Z Machine that could generate the kind
  of magnetic fields required to drive the engine - say they may
  carry out a test if the theory withstands further scrutiny."
  Nope, sorry, wrong. "[F]urther scrutiny"? Why, what scrutiny has
  the theory withstood so far? And if you go back to the
  "scientists" in question, namely to Roger Lenard from Sandia
  National Laboratories who is quoted in the New Scientist
  article, you'll find that he doesn't talk about further scrutiny
  either:
  "For now, though, Lenard considers the theory too shaky to
  justify the use of the Z machine. "I would be very interested in
  getting Sandia interested if we could get a more perspicacious
  introduction to the mathematics behind the proposed experiment,"
  he says."
  ...in other words, and put very politely, could someone please
  write this theory down in a comprehensible manner before we
  think about bringing a rather expensive piece of research
  equipment into play?
  Ah, well. So much for New Scientist's, and The Scotsman's,
  standards of science reporting.

  Markus Poessel

                                              Red Rain Phenomenon Of Kerala ET?
  From: William Wise <will.nul>
  Date: Sat, 07 Jan 2006 07:54:34 -0500
  Fwd Date: Sat, 07 Jan 2006 08:30:43 -0500
  Subject: Red Rain Phenomenon Of Kerala ET?

  Source: Astrophysics and Space Science
  http://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0601022
  -----
  Astrophysics, abstract
  astro-ph/0601022
  From: Godfrey Louis [view email]
  Date: Mon, 2 Jan 2006 07:54:10 GMT                       (461kb)
  The red rain phenomenon of Kerala and its possible
  extraterrestrial origin
  Authors: Godfrey Louis, A. Santhosh Kumar (Mahatma Gandhi
  University, Kottayam, India)
  Comments: 18 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in
  Astrophysics and Space Science

  A red rain phenomenon occurred in Kerala, India starting from
  25th July 2001, in which the rainwater appeared coloured in
  various localized places that are spread over a few hundred
  kilometers in Kerala.
  Maximum cases were reported during the first 10 days and
  isolated cases were found to occur for about 2 months.
  The striking red colouration of the rainwater was found to be
  due to the suspension of microscopic red particles having the
  appearance of biological cells. These particles have no
  similarity with usual desert dust.
  An estimated minimum quantity of 50,000 kg of red particles has
  fallen from the sky through red rain.
  An analysis of this strange phenomenon further shows that the
  conventional atmospheric transport processes like dust storms
  etc. cannot explain this phenomenon.
  The electron microscopic study of the red particles shows fine
  cell structure indicating their biological cell like nature.
  EDAX analysis shows that the major elements present in these
  cell like particles are carbon and oxygen.
  Strangely, a test for DNA using Ethidium Bromide dye
  fluorescence technique indicates absence of DNA in these cells.
  In the context of a suspected link between a meteor airburst
  event and the red rain, the possibility for the extraterrestrial
  origin of these particles from cometary fragments is discussed.
  -----
  Will

  Subject: Aliens Drop In To Lend Us A Hand



  Source: The Sydney Morning Herald - Australia
  http://tinyurl.com/76edb
  January 7, 2006

  Aliens Drop In To Lend Us A Hand
  By Sunanda Creagh
  His hair is pasted down with rain, his umbrella is wonky and his
  shoes are wet. But Tony Oursler soldiers on through the drizzle.
  Despite his expression, the New York video artist may even be
  having fun. After two years of planning, Oursler's alien-themed
  video projection Blue Invasion opens in Hyde Park tonight.
  "When you have something that you plan for a place 5000 miles
  from home, some of it's done on paper, some of it's in your
  imagination. Now it's in real life," Oursler said at a Blue
  Invasion rehearsal on Thursday, when technicians worked through
  the rain to project talking faces, sound and colour onto the
  Archibald Fountain.
  Tonight is the first public display of Blue Invasion, and it
  marks the real beginning of the month-long Sydney Festival. The
  festival's director, Fergus Linehan, is relieved it has finally
  started - not without last minute mishaps, of course. Like the
  near-death experience of one Sydney Festival drawcard, the
  creator of The Andersen Project, Robert Lepage.
  "Poor Robert Lepage. His plane's engine blew up when they were
  taking off from Honolulu [on Wednesday]. They looked out the
  window and there were flames coming out of the engine," Linehan
  said. After an emergency landing and a second, more successful,
  take-off, Lepage was Sydney-bound.
  Then there was the Russian theatre company temporarily stranded
  in Kuala Lumpur airport after a cancelled flight. "Oh yeah, and
  the meteor fell off a truck," said Linehan, gesturing at a huge
  part of Oursler's work.
  For Sydneysiders, the fun has just begun. For Linehan, it's
  almost over. "Once it's over, it's so over - that's the bizarre
  thing about festivals. The day before it finishes, I can pick up
  the phone and get anyone on the phone - anybody. The day after,
  no one wants to know about you."

  From: UFO UpDates - Toronto <ufoupdates.nul>

  Fwd Date: Sat, 07 Jan 2006 09:45:46 -0500
  Subject: My Roswell Alien Experience



  Source: The Gridley Herald - Gridley, California, USA
  http://www.gridleyherald.com/articles/2006/01/06/community/news02.txt
  Jan 06, 2006

  Scotty Sez.....
  By Scotty Williams
  My Roswell Alien Experience
  Since moving to New Mexico my wife and I have made a
  constructive effort to expose our children to some of the many
  cultural experiences available here.
  This summer we visited the White Sands Missile Range, where more
  has been done to perfect America's art of blowing things up than
  the Terminator movies.
  We have also visited the mighty Rio Ruidoso (translation: noisy
  river) which, if it were located in California, would be the
  state's smallest river (translation: quarter the size of most
  drainage ditches). Rio Ruidoso is one of New Mexico's finer
  trout streams, not only because it's easy to cross (just step
  over), but because it trickles year round.
  And of course we live within 100 miles of the famous Trinity
  Site, where the first atomic bomb was tested.
  In addition to the sense of cultural this brings to our front
  door, we also don't have to pay for electricity since the ground
  now produces it's own.
  Just stuff the end of an extension cord into the sand and you're
  good to go!
  But for some reason my family and I had failed to take in what
  is easily New Mexico's biggest cultural center, the
  International UFO Museum and Research Center located in Roswell.
  We remedied this oversight on Monday.
  For those of you who do not own "The Roswell Alien Autopsy
  Collector's Edition," Roswell was the site of the most famous
  UFO crash in history.
  In July of 1947 a couple of outer space visitors, who had
  apparently partied too hard the night before, crashed their
  craft.
  Several witnesses, who may or may not have attended the same
  party, claimed not only to have seen the craft, but the bodies
  of two space aliens.
  An alleged government cover-up ensued, as did the plots for
  several science fiction movies.



http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m07-011.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:36]
My Roswell Alien Experience

  The official government explanation is that the only thing that
  crashed in the desert that day was a weather balloon.
  I don't know what to believe either way, but having viewed the
  sparse landscape around Roswell it would be pretty difficult to
  mistake a weather balloon for a flying saucer and rocks for a
  couple of aliens in flight suits.
  The land is so barren around Roswell that it would be impossible
  to mistake the figure of a person from two miles away.
  My take on the Roswell crash is either the folks who witnessed
  this event had the foresight to know such a story would allow
  the city to sell thousands of dollars worth of inflatable aliens
  a year or there is some type of governmental cover-up.
  I'm a bit of an expert on space aliens since I've been abducted
  numerous times, usually while shopping at Kmart.
  One minute I'm in line and the next I see a blue light and I
  lose consciousness. I awake feeling as though I've been
  trampled.
  At the International UFO Museum and Research Center the lady at
  the front desk was also savvy to both alien abduction techniques
  and government cover-ups.
  Right off she solicited a $2 "donation" from each of us. This
  whole mandatory donation concept bothered me. Is it really a
  donation if it's required to gain admission?
  I didn't argue the point because I make it a policy to never
  offend any group that may have access to extraterrestrial
  technology. Besides the lady at the front desk informed me that
  the money is going to good cause, the construction of a new
  building on the curator's home planet.
  In addition to selling inflatable aliens and "I was prodded in
  Roswell" T-shirts, the museum provides a lot of evidence
  supporting the existence of UFOs and the little green fellas
  that pilot them.
  In the general area of the museum are also several gift shops
  specializing in alien souvenirs. It's clear a poorly piloted
  alien spacecraft has meant quite an economic boom for Roswell.
  The city even has an Annual Roswell UFO Festival complete with
  "live-action alien puppet shows" and a ?K/10K Alien Chase Walk
  or Fun Run."
  As for ourselves we came, we saw, we took pictures and bought a
  few alien trinkets for the road. While there we wanted to eat
  somewhere that showed the unique character of Roswell.
  We were tempted by Arby's sign, which read "Aliens Welcome," but
  instead settled for McDonald's, which featured a saucer shaped
  playground.
  Before heading home, we visited the Bottomless Lakes State Park,
  located 12 miles east of Roswell.
  The park features several lakes that are far deeper than they
  are wide. For a mere $5 "donation" you can tour each of the
  lakes. The "donation" registration form prominently states, "no
  refunds." This is probably due to the fact that each of the
  lakes does in fact have a bottom.
  "Obviously there is a bottom or all the water would run out,"
  the park ranger informed me.
  The deepest of the lakes is 90 feet to the bottom. It's a
  popular scuba diving spot in the spring and summer months.
  According to the literature, the bottomless lakes have been a
  source of interest for many years. In the old west days cowboys
  have claimed to have spotted mermaids in the lakes-which
  testifies to how lonely a fella can get on the open range.
  Others claim things lost in the lakes (such as Dennis Rodman's
  career) have been recovered in the famous Carlsbad Caverns some
  80 miles away.



http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m07-011.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:36]
My Roswell Alien Experience

  Overall Roswell was worth the time to visit. If ever this way
  I'd be happy to show you around, for a minimum "donation" of
  course.
  (Scotty Sez... appears in The Gridley Herald each Friday and can
  also be read online at: www.gridleyherald.com).

  own conclusion while rejecting relatively hard evidence.

  recognize "intelligent transformation." ( Could be" intelligent
  design" in the first place!) What is the baseline against which
  the transformation could be measured?

  any merit? And the pseudoscientific argument against UFO data as
  ET mounted by SETI people and, frankly, ignorant skeptics
  amounts to Non potest, ergo non est (It can't be, therefore it
  isn't) pure and simple. No, I still think Fermi's SWAG has no
  merit other than perhaps as an intellectual exercise.
  - Dick

  BTW - I would like to change the heading of this discussion to:
  ET does solve the Fermi Paradox; in fact, it falsifies its
  premise.

  Martin,
  I think the above is an outstanding commentary. I would add that
  Fermi was a scientist's scientist. This became clear to me in
  listening to comments by other U. of Chicago profs when Fermi
  died in late 1954... I went to Chicago in Sept. of 1953.
  He was not simple minded. He was well known for using questions
  as a teaching tool in an attempt to unlock the secrets of the
  universe and the thinking of students. He was one of very few who
  were adept at both experimentation and theory.
  We have no idea what he did or didn't know about UFOs. He did
  have a very high level security clearance and had close
  connections with Los Alamos where I am convinced some of the
  Roswell wreckage was sent.
  Certainly we do not yet have any indication of how much aliens
  have transformed other solar systems in the local neighborhood
  or in the universe.
  Just look around the solar system and see how much change there
  has been in our understanding of the surfaces of the other
  planets as our observing tools have been sharpened by space
  exploration. Our knowledge of the local galactic neighborhood...
  say out 55 light years... is miniscule.
  The need for Dyson spheres has no theoretical or practical basis
  especially when local travel is feasible.
  There are fat reports including one from a congressional service
  listing totally nonsensical statements (by well educated and
  very ignorant scientists)made about what is possible and how
  the universe operates. Fermi was not one of those.

  >In response to Cathy and Martin, I think you are mistaken about
  >the two options for a stable state. Illogical though it might
  >sound, I think that chaos is a third stable state!
  Wonderful. Another spectacular example of missing the point. Do
  you know what chaos is? All of celestial dynamics is about
  chaotic systems. The whole point about chaotic systems is not
  that they just do any old thing, but that they tend inevitably
  over time towards the system attractor state. Catastrophic
  chaotic systems are exquisitely sensitive to initial conditions,
  and because of this are driven to extremal states which are
  dynamically stable.
  And this is the exact _point_ of the Fermi argument, as
  expressed by Cathy Reason: Non-zero initial conditions trigger
  chaotic oscillations towards an extremal state which is the
  system "attractor". The so-called strange attractors of chaotic
  systems are those which describe just that type of self-similar
  fractal proliferation which is so characteristic of the way
  organic systems on Earth grow and spread.
  >Although there may appear to be stability when viewed over an
  >extremely long time period (Millions of Millions of years),
  ... since this is in the order of 1000 times the age of the
  universe I think you might be speculating...
  >when
  >examined in smaller but at least for humanity, very significant
  >time periods (in the order of say a hundred thousand years),
  >parts of the universe are in a state of flux.
  All of the universe is always in a state of flux. It is
  precisely dynamical flux that generates and maintains the
  structural stability that we see. This appears to be true as
  much of human societal and informational complex systems as it
  is true of other biological, chemical and physical ones. Where
  do you get 100,000 years from as some sort of constant churn
  rate for arbitrary "parts of the universe"? Significant physical
  changes in stars and galaxies occur on all timescales as far as
  we can see from milliseconds to billions of years.
  Your figure is apparently suggested as an important timespan in
  human history, but it is not scale or magnitude that you should
  be trying to transfer from the particular to the universal,
  rather it is the underlying dynamical structure and its drivers.
  When you do this you find that your most robust, because most


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m08-001.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:42]
Re: ETH Does Not Solve The Fermi Paradox - Shough

  general, expectations about other evolved technical cultures will
  be those that most generally apply across the living systems that
  we know from humanity to slime moulds.
  The reason generality is important is exactly _because_ of those
  small and short-timescale variables (which you mention below)
  that we don't want to allow to dominate our projections. You
  might think these variations therefore get smoothed out on the
  grand scale, so that the technology-dominated universe would get
  very uniform; after all, I said that planetary dynamics was
  about chaotic systems, and we have regular eclipses, and Saturn
  has those nice neat rings. But organic systems do not behave
  like these mechanical systems. As with the analogous "B-Z
  reaction" in chemistry, it is the _uniform_distribution that is
  unstable.
  There is some evidence that the cosmic structure on galaxy
  cluster scales is a fractal, but we don't tend to see this
  because the gravitational system attractors are so very close to
  those of classical dynamical systems on local scales. These
  attractors are closed period cycles or loops in phase space,
  echoed in the actual orbital dynamics that we see. To try to
  think of ET technological expansion in these terms would be to
  adopt the simplistic conventional notion of "colonisation"
  (properly criticised by Dick Hall) where a local behaviour gets
  disseminated and imposed everywhere. There is real doubt IMO
  (another story!) that this even the proper approach to
  understanding "universal constants" in physics; in a cultural-
  biological context I'm sure it's inappropriate. But this doesn't
  mean that more chaotic behaviour has no system descriptors.
  The characteristic of chaotic attractor states is that they are
  really complex fractals, with lots of self-similar convergences
  and divergences going on at all scales. The attractor state is
  turbulent and has a lot of unpredictability in it. It is not a
  smooth average. Fractal systems do not actually have valid
  representations as isotropic and homogeneous states. This
  suggests that the most likely result of proliferating
  technological activity across the cosmos, based on biological
  and general dynamical systems theory models that we know about,
  is that it will have lots of visible variation in degree and in
  kind, in both time and space. Even if we can't necessarily know
  how to distinguish between the effects of nature and technology
  when we study phenomena on cosmic scales, I suggest that
  anisotropy and inhomogeneity would be one indicator of large
  scale technological expansion.
  So this is one other way of looking at the Fermi Paradox:
  Instead of asking, "Why don't we see signs of technology
  transforming the universe everywhere we look?" a better question
  might be, "Why does the degree and character of technological
  transformation of the universe look so similar everywhere?" Two
  possible answers are that the degree of transformation is 0% or
  100%.
  The 0% option seems hard to defend. Statistically we have good
  reason to suspect that we are primitives. After all we know of
  only one technological species, which in the space of just a few
  thousand years has progressed from throwing rocks to beginning
  to physically modify the near-Earth environment, has shown the
  amazing chutzpah of mapping the power spectrum of the act of
  creation, and has already seriously considered planetary re-
  engineering in its own star system. Imagine a million other
  species, with a million times the evolutionary timescale
  available to them.
  So maybe, counterintuitively, 100% transformation is actually
  more likely than 0%. If it is 100% then the degree of isotropy
  and homogeneity suggests that the observable universe is
  possibly a locally uniform fluctuation in a _phase_space that
  contains a chaotic spectrum of other universes in other states
  of transformation. I say "phase space" but this could arguably
  be consistent with some modern cosmological theories that
  propose types of anthropic "evolutionary selection" among a
  multiverse of superspace domains with different dimensional
  characteristics, possibly different fundamental constants and
  different physics.
  >There are so many variable factors when history and the
  >development of the universe is observed in relatively short
  >timescale that it is highly unlikely in my view that similar

  They are indeed likely to have much more evolutionary history
  under their belt, as you say say, and to have done even more of
  what organisms tend to do: expand, adapt and survive. If they
  are as similar to us as technological chimpanzees (we are of
  course assuming creatures with advanced technology for this
  discussion, else they could not be here and would have no List
  and no debate) then it's game, set and match for Fermi!
  Your criticism relies on them being much more different from us

  details of culture, technology, morals - the fact that your
  aliens have anything approximating these categories of
  description is sufficient for us to justify a working hypothesis
  that they are analogous organisms to us, in the sense that say

  >Any ET intelligence does not only have the advantage of longer
  >evolution, but will almost certainly have a completely different
  >evolutionary path to our own. Putting that into a terrestrial

  >human behaviour and values.
  No, we don't need to predict behaviour and values that are
  significantly different from our Coelocanth behaviour and
  values. Knowing that we are organic, energy-consuming, far-from-
  equilibrium systems would be enough for the Coelocanth to know
  all it needs to know. We are very closely related to Coelocanths
  in terms of those old-brain instincts and motivations that the
  Coelocanth is going to be thinking about. In fishy terms, he
  would see us as territorial predatory competitors for ocean
  space and whitebait or angler fish or whatever, and that's
  exactly what we are.
  Here we are talking about what we know of the common properties
  of all life from humans to bacteria, generalised to dynamical
  systems theory within which living systems are themselves a
  special case of complex systems. As we know nothing a priori
  about ET this is proper conservative reasoning.
  >All that we can do is speculate, but

  Hi Don,
  Thanks for the input. Yes, I've long been aware of the early
  saucer nests, etc. ... I think there may be some overlap when it
  comes to the simplest circles and rings (a common phenomenon,
  often UFO related?), but the more complex ones are a different
  matter, I agree (mostly man-made now I think, not all perhaps,
  but the majority; see my notes below).
  I wish there were more details also. I included it as a report
  as it is of circular flattened vegetation in a field, not
  (apparently) missing or "burned" plants, soil or ice, etc. (all
  of which we've had in Canada also, as you probably know). I
  don't claim either that there is any connection between crop
  circles and UFOs, as some will insist, but other researchers
  have been finding more and more old cases like this, sometimes
  in more detail, of flattened circles (sometimes swirled),
  sometimes associated with UFOs (like Langenburg, Saskatchewan in
  1974). These ones are very similar to the "first" early crop
  circles in England in the 70s and 80s, and all very simple.
  That's one of the reasons I've found myself in later years
  tending to agree more with people like Colin Andrews, Freddy
  Silva, Paul Vigay, etc. that the majority of genuine formations
  probably have always been the simpler ones, which, as it
  happens, are still common in some places outside of the UK, like
  the prairies here, for example. We _still_ get simpler circles,
  in the same geographic regions, that are virtually identical to
  ones from many years before, in various physical details. And
  with the many I've looked at now in western Canada, the ones
  that have often been the most impressive (quality, complexity of

  lay, lack of damage, physical deformities) have again been the
  simpler ones. Mind you, it has been some of the formations in
  9'-10' tall cattle corn, mostly geometric and up to 300 feet
  long, which had the very pronounced nodal deformities (by the
  hundreds, per formation)... see also The Scientific Evidence
  page on the CCCRN web site.
  Re the formation archives on the web site, I include any
  circular or geometric formations that are simply flattened in
  vegetation. Others that are burned or missing vegetation (even
  if circular), or in soil, ice, etc. I keep separate (but do have
  filed reports going back to at least 1880). The latest (and
  impressive) ice circle in Ontario from December 9, 2005 is a
  good example. See also Related Phenomena on the web site for
  more on these kinds of cases (as I note there, "related" just in
  the sense of being usually circular, at least).

  Hi Eleanor,
  Wikipedia says "no" for human red cells and DNA - here's the quote:
  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell
  Red blood cells are also known as RBCs or erythrocytes (from
  Greek erythros for "red" and kytos for "hollow," nowadays
  translated as "cell"). A schistocyte is a red blood cell
  undergoing fragmentation, or a fragmented part of a red blood
  cell.
  Mammalian erythrocytes
  Erythrocytes in mammals are anucleate when mature, meaning that
  they don't have a cell nucleus and thus no DNA. (The erythrocytes
  of nearly all other vertebrates have nuclei; the only known
  exception is salamanders of the Batrachoseps genus.) Erythrocytes
  also lose their other organelles including their mitochondria and
  produce energy by fermentation, via glycolysis of glucose
  followed by lactic acid production. Like most cell types, red
  cells do not have an insulin receptor and thus glucose uptake is
  not regulated by insulin."
  And, just because I got a similar question on that red rain today
  and so did the search, here's part of my own reply -
  "If carbon and oxygen are the most significant cell materials,
  that's in line with the most common elements found in deep space:
  CHON - carbon, hydrogen (in the `rain') oxygen + nitrogen (maybe
  also in the `rain')
  PLUS deep space has clouds of molecular materials - significantly
  the 20 or so amino acids necessary for life on Earth! - which
  could explain the "organic" nature of the cells.
  Got that last from interesting book maybe called "Stardust" by
  John Gribbin which closely examines the nuclear processes and
  supernova events that make up the elements (which we need) seen
  around the universe. Seems that `organic' stuff is amazingly
  abundant in regions of deep space.
  I'm slightly inclined to agree with your authors linking of the
  rain with the meteorite explosion - since the "solids" (not
  hydrogen or oxygen in gaseous form) would need a casing to
  protect them entering the atmosphere, and the explosion would
  explain the elliptical dispersal zone.

There's More To North Star Than Meets The Eye




                                                          UFO Updates
                                   A mailing list for the study of UFO-related phenomena
                                               'Its All Here In Black & White'
    Location: UFOUpDatesList.Com > 2006 > Jan > Jan 9

                                     There's More To North Star Than Meets The Eye
  From: NASA News <hqnews.nul>
  Date: Mon, 9 Jan 2006 09:43:37 -0500 (EST)
  Fwd Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2006 19:09:41 -0500
  Subject: There's More To North Star Than Meets The Eye

  Jan. 9, 2006
  Erica Hupp
  Headquarters, Washington
  (202) 358-1237
  Donna Weaver
  Space Telescope Science Institute, Baltimore
  (410) 338-4493
  David Aguilar
  Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, Cambridge, Mass.
  (617) 495-7462
  RELEASE: 06-004
  There's More To The North Star Than Meets The Eye
  By stretching the capabilities of NASA's Hubble Space Telescope
  to the limit, astronomers photographed the close companion to
  Polaris, known also as the North Star, for the first time.
  "Hubble's exceptional pointing capabilities combined with the
  wonderful performance of its instruments allow scientists to see
  the universe in finer detail than ever before," said Michael
  Moore, NASA's Hubble program executive. "It is that clear vision
  that makes these types of images possible," he added.
  The North Star is thought to be a steady, solitary point of
  light that guided sailors for ages, but there is more to this
  star than meets the eye. The North Star is actually a triple
  star system. While one companion is easily viewed with small
  telescopes, the other hugs Polaris so tightly that it has never
  been seen until now.
  "The star we observed is so close to Polaris that we needed
  every available bit of Hubble's resolution to see it," said
  astronomer Nancy Evans of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for
  Astrophysics, Cambridge, Mass. The companion proved to be less
  than two-tenths of an arcsecond from Polaris. That is an
  incredibly tiny angle equivalent to the apparent diameter of a
  quarter located 19 miles away. At the system's distance of 430
  light-years from Earth, that translates into a separation of
  about 2 billion miles.
  "The brightness difference between the two stars made it even
  more difficult to resolve them," said astronomer Howard Bond of
  the Space Telescope Science Institute, Baltimore. Polaris is a
  super-giant more than two thousand times brighter than the sun,
  while its companion is a dwarf star. "With Hubble, we've pulled
  the North Star's companion out of the shadows and into the
  spotlight," he said.
  "Our ultimate goal is to get the accurate mass for Polaris,"
  Evans said. "To do that, the next milestone is to measure the
  motion of the companion in its orbit," she added. Astronomers
  want to determine the mass of Polaris, because it is the nearest
  Cepheid variable star. Cepheids' brightness variations are used
  to measure the distances of galaxies and the expansion rate of


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m09-012.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:53]
There's More To North Star Than Meets The Eye

  the universe. It is essential to understand their intrinsic
  physics makeup and evolution. Knowing their mass is the most
  important ingredient in this understanding.
  The researchers plan to continue observing the Polaris system
  for several years. The movement of the small companion during
  its 30-year orbit around the primary should be detectable. The
  researchers presented their data today during the 207th meeting
  of the American Astronomical Society in Washington.
  The Hubble Space Telescope is a project of international
  cooperation between NASA and the European Space Agency. The
  Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore conducts Hubble
  science operations. The Institute is operated for NASA by the
  Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, Inc.,
  Washington.
  For images and additional information about this research on the
  Web, visit:
  http://hubblesite.org/news/2006/02


  For information about NASA and agency programs on the Web, visit:
  http://www.nasa.gov/home

  -end-

Edison's 'Conquest Of Mars'




                                                          UFO Updates
                                   A mailing list for the study of UFO-related phenomena
                                               'Its All Here In Black & White'
    Location: UFOUpDatesList.Com > 2006 > Jan > Jan 9

                                                      Edison's 'Conquest Of Mars'
  From: Nick Balaskas <Nikolaos.nul>
  Date: Mon, 9 Jan 2006 11:45:33 -0500 (Eastern Standard Time)
  Fwd Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2006 19:14:48 -0500
  Subject: Edison's 'Conquest Of Mars'

  Hi Everyone!
  I got to hear and meet with Robert Godwin, publisher of Apogee
  Books, when he gave a talk last Wednesday to the members of the
  Toronto Centre of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada at
  the Ontario Science Centre last Wednesday.
  Godwin gave many examples of long forgotten works of science
  fiction and scientific speculations by astronomers from the late
  19th and early 20th centuries that not only directly influenced
  many of the space scientists and engineers of this generation
  that got us to the Moon and shaped our ideas about Mars but who
  also played a part in creating our present beliefs about aliens
  and UFOs.
  Many of us are familiar with H.G. Wells 1897 'War of the World'
  that created panic when it was first broadcast on radio in 1938
  and later popularized in several films, including Steven
  Spielberg's version that was in the cinemas last summer, but few
  know that the Hearst publishing empire commissioned a sequel in
  1898 called 'Edison's Conquest of Mars' that was serialized in
  their many newspapers. In this sequel, an armada of manmade
  cigar shaped UFOs were built and first test flown to the Moon
  before this 19th century international financed human invasion
  of Mars was launched from Earth (sounds familiar?). Now for the

  from the FAS Project on Government Secrecy

  **           CRS ON AUTHORIZATION FOR USE OF MILITARY FORCE

  CRS ON AUTHORIZATION FOR USE OF MILITARY FORCE
  The legislative history of the September 14, 2001 Congressional
  resolution authorizing the use of force in response to the
  September 11 attacks is concisely examined in a new report of
  the Congressional Research Service.
  The 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force, or AUMF, has
  been in the news lately because the Bush Administration has
  claimed that it provided statutory authority for the National
  Security Agency to conduct warrantless surveillance within the
  United States, a claim that has been disputed by some in
  Congress and elsewhere.
  The new CRS legislative history notes that the White House had
  initially sought legislative authority "to deter and pre-empt
  any future acts of terrorism or aggression against the United
  States."
  But "This language would have seemingly authorized the
  President, without durational limitation, and at his sole
  discretion, to take military action against any nation,
  terrorist group or individuals in the world without having to
  seek further authority from the
  Congress."
  "It would have granted the President open-ended authority to act
  against all terrorism and terrorists or potential aggressors
  against the United States anywhere, not just the authority to
  act against the terrorists involved in the September 11, 2001
  attacks, and those nations, organizations and persons who had
  aided or harbored the terrorists.
  "As a consequence, this portion of the language in the proposed
  White House draft resolution was strongly opposed by key
  legislators in Congress and was not included in the final
  version of the legislation that was passed," the CRS explained.
  A copy of the new CRS publication was obtained by Secrecy News.
  See "Authorization For Use Of Military Force in Response to the
  9/11 Attacks (P.L. 107-40): Legislative History," January 4,
  2006:
  http://www.fas.org/sgp/crs/natsec/RS22357.pdf




http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m09-015.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:55]
Secrecy News -- 01/09/06

  CRS ON DECLARATIONS OF WAR AND AUMFS
  The distinction between a formal declaration of war and an
  authorization for use of military force was addressed in an
  exceptionally informative report of the Congressional Research
  Service in 2003.
  "With respect to domestic law, a declaration of war
  automatically brings into effect numerous standby statutory
  authorities conferring special powers on the President with
  respect to the military, foreign trade, transportation,
  communications, manufacturing, alien enemies, etc."
  "In contrast, no standby authorities appear to be triggered
  automatically by an authorization for the use of force."
  The history of both categories is delineated, including the
  texts of the eleven formal declarations of war and the most
  important authorizations for use of military force, along with
  an itemization of the various statutes that are triggered
  directly or indirectly in each case.
  The 112 page CRS report is not generally available in the public
  domain. A copy was obtained by Secrecy News.
  See "Declarations of War and Authorizations for the Use of
  Military Force: Historical Background and Legal Implications,"
  updated January 14, 2003:
  http://www.fas.org/sgp/crs/natsec/RL31133.pdf

  MORTON HALPERIN ON WARRANTLESS NSA SURVEILLANCE
  "The warrantless National Security Agency (NSA) surveillance
  program is an illegal and unnecessary intrusion into the privacy
  of all Americans," writes Morton H. Halperin in a new assessment
  of the controversial program.
  Halperin, a leading civil libertarian and former Pentagon and
  State Department official, played an influential role in the
  enactment of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of
  1978, which subjected intelligence surveillance within the
  United States to a measure of judicial oversight. He also has
  the distinction of having his phone tapped at the direction of
  Henry Kissinger, who eventually apologized for the action.
  "Congress must conduct hearings to determine exactly what is
  being done in the new NSA program and why the administration
  concluded that it could not use FISA," he urged.
  "Then it should determine what needs to be done to insure that,
  in the future, Presidents obey the law."
  See "A Legal Analysis of the NSA Warrantless Surveillance
  Program" by Morton H. Halperin, January 6, 2006:
  http://www.americanprogress.org/site/pp.asp?c=biJRJ8OVF&b=133446
  9

  STEPHEN CAMBONE ON DOD FACILITY SECURITY
  Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Stephen A. Cambone
  has issued a new Department of Defense Instruction on the
  subject of DoD facility security.
  "The authority of a DoD commander to take reasonably necessary
  and lawful measures to maintain law and order and to protect
  installation personnel and property ... shall not be exercised
  in an arbitrary, unpredictable or discriminatory manner."
  See DoD Instruction 5200.08, "Security of DoD Installations and
  Resources," December 10, 2005:
  http://www.fas.org/irp/doddir/dod/i5200_08.pdf

                                                           Is Lovekin A General?
  From: UFO UpDates - Toronto <ufoupdates.nul>
  Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2006 21:43:47 -0500
  Fwd Date: Mon, 09 Jan 2006 21:43:47 -0500
  Subject: Is Lovekin A General?



  Source: Kevin Randle's Blog
  http://kevinrandle.blogspot.com/
  Posted: Thursday, January 05, 2006

  Thursday, January 05, 2006
  Is Lovekin A General
  When I came across the name of Brigadier General Stephen L.
  Lovekin in both the Dr. Stephen Greer Disclosure Project and
  later used by Dr. Michael Salla for his Exopolitics studies, I
  was interested. Thanks to a book entitled Stolen Valor I=92m now
  suspicious of most claims of military association, especially
  those who claim to have achieved high rank. It surprised me then
  and continues to surprise me that so many people will claim
  military service who have never worn a uniform and that so many
  of those who were actually in the military have embellished
  their careers.
  The information available from both the Disclosure Project and
  Exopolitics suggested that as a young officer, Lovekin had
  served in the Eisenhower White House. According to what Lovekin
  said, and which was related by others, Lovekin worked directly
  under President Eisenhower in May of 1959 in the White House
  Army Signaling Agency and later under Kennedy with an above top-
  secret clearance.
  Lovekin himself explained how he had learned of the Roswell UFO
  crash and seen a piece of the debris. He said, "One afternoon
  when we were just about ready to finish up training, Colonel
  Holomon brought out a piece of what appeared to be metallic
  debris. He went on to explain that this was material that had
  come from a New Mexico crash in 1947 of an extraterrestrial
  craft, and that was discussed at length=85."
  Finally, he said, "But what happened was that Eisenhower got
  sold out. He realized that he was losing control of the UFO
  subject. He realized that the phenomenon was not going to be in
  the best hands."
  This is important stuff, if it could be confirmed. A general
  officer, one who had once held the ear of the president and who
  could report on the president=92s interest in UFOs, would make an
  impressive witness, especially if he could talk of a UFO crash
  and recovered debris. It should be relatively simple to verify
  Lovekin=92s credentials as a general.
  With general officers, unlike those in the lower officer grades,
  the military keeps good records, their biographies are often
  posted at various web sites, and many people know and remember
  them. But, those on-line sites, while having the biographies of
  many generals, including some obscure ones such as Martin F.
  Scanlon, who died many years ago, Arthur Exon who died last
  summer, and many prominent ones such as former Air Force Chief


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m09-018.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:56]
Is Lovekin A General?

  of Staff Nathan Twining and Lieutenant General Roger Ramey,
  contained nothing about Stephen Lovekin. I checked on how
  comprehensive these sites were by typing in the names of some of
  the National Guard generals I know and they appeared as well.
  But not Lovekin.
  I tried the Army Register, which contained the names of all
  officers serving in the Army and found nothing for Lovekin. Then
  again, I tried Corso who we all know was an Army officer and
  didn=92t find him either. I don=92t know why Corso wasn=92t included
  in the years that covered his military service. What that told
  me was that somehow officers were left out.
  I tried the National Guard Bureau. It would seem they would know
  the names of all officers who reached flag rank in the National
  Guard. They had no listing for Lovekin, but also said that prior
  to 1995, their records were sometimes incomplete. It meant that
  Lovekin could have again slipped through the crack. I don=92t
  believe this likely, but they made it clear that there are a few
  gaps in their information.
  Lovekin, in his biography, claimed that he had been a JAG
  officer, and most everyone believed him to have served with the
  North Carolina National Guard. Joe Stefula attempted to learn
  about this through the Office of the Adjutant General, but
  apparently found nothing or received no reply. I tried a number
  of different angles, and learned that JAG officers are not
  promoted to brigadier general in North Carolina and there has
  never been a JAG general in the state. North Carolina does not
  brevet their officers one grade upon retirement, so a colonel,
  serving as JAG would not be promoted to brigadier general when
  he retired. There is no record of a brigadier general named
  Lovekin, in any Army branch (the JAG being just one branch, like
  Infantry or Military Police) in North Carolina.
  Then there was the claim by Lovekin that he worked in the
  Eisenhower White House. Well, if Stephen L. Lovekin and the
  attorney in North Carolina are the same man, this makes little
  sense. According to the information Stephen L. Lovekin, the
  attorney, was born in August 1940. His biography at the law firm
  web site does not mention any military service, nor does it
  suggest that he was ever a brigadier general. That in and of
  itself seems strange.
  To further complicate the matter, if these are the same men,
  then Lovekin was 18 when he worked in the Eisenhower White
  House. While it is not unheard of for a teenager to be an Army
  officer (I was a warrant officer at 19), it is extremely
  unlikely that someone of that age to be assigned to the White
  House. Those postings are normally reserved for more experienced
  soldiers.
  Once again, if we read Lovekin=92s law biography carefully, we
  find no time for him to have been trained and then serve as an
  Army officer, complete his under graduate training and then
  attend law school. He received his law degree in 1964. He would
  have had to graduate from high school in 1957 or 1958, complete
  OCS which, in that time frame lasted six months, serve his
  military term, attend college and then go on to law school, all
  in six or seven years.
  So, it seems unlikely that Stephen Lovekin is, or was, a
  brigadier general with the active duty force, with the National
  Guard, or in the Army Reserve. There simply is no record of it
  anywhere that I can find. But, there is one solution that might
  work.
  During World War II, all the state National Guards were
  activated and called to active duty for extended periods. To
  compensate for the loss, the states created another state
  militia. In Iowa it was called the Iowa State Guard. This
  organization, sanctioned by the state was a semi-military group
  that took on the roles of the National Guard.
  At the end of the war, many of these organizations ceased to
  exist. Some had their charters expire, others simply had their
  membership siphoned off into the regular Guard, and some were
  officially disbanded.
  For the last fifteen or twenty years there has been an effort to
  recreate these state guards. In Iowa, they have no official


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/jan/m09-018.shtml[10/12/2011 10:15:56]
Is Lovekin A General?

  status, though they do wear the standard Battle Dress Uniform
  (BDU) of the Army, wear the same rank insignia, and claim to
  require the same type of training. They are not authorized to
  wear the Iowa National Guard patch, and they are required to
  wear another patch that suggests they are the Iowa State Guard,
  as opposed to the Iowa National Guard. Their uniforms say "Iowa
  State Guard," while those of the National Guard say, "US Army."
  These state guards have been pulled together in an unofficial
  national organization of state militia. Lovekin might hold his
  brigadier general commission in just such an organization. It
  might suggest his claim to be a brigadier general, while
  unofficial and not recognized by either the Army or the North
  Carolina National Guard would allow him to claim the rank. This
  is all speculation on my part.
  This all suggests to me that the "whistle blower" testimony
  offered by Stephen L. Lovekin is of little use in developing any
  policies related to UFOs or extraterrestrial visitation. There
  is no corroboration of his many claims of military service as a
  high-ranking officer, no verification of his positions in the
  White House and little reason to believe he was witness to the
  things he claims. Like so many of the other whistle blowers, he
  should be removed from our lists.

  [Thanks to Stuart Miller of http://www.uforeview.net for the lead]

  <snip>
  >This is what I was getting at when I said that the ETH does not
  >solve the Fermi Paradox. The way I've always heard the story
  >told, Fermi asked the question because he had been thinking
  >about models of interstellar migration. We know the average
  >distances between stars, the approximate number of stars in the
  >galaxy and so forth, so we can do some basic calculations if we
  >make some assumptions about the speed of starships, the amount
  >of time a new colony must develop before it can launch ships of
  >its own, etc. Even if we use very conservative assumptions, such
  >as limiting starship speeds to a small fraction of the speed of
  >light and assuming many centuries must pass before a planet can
  >start sending out its own colonists, these models predict that
  >it should be possible for a single starfaring civilization to
  >colonize the galaxy within a period of time of a few tens of
  >millions of years. That's the blink of an eye compared to the
  >age of the galaxy.
  >Basically the only assumptions we are making with this model is
  >that a hypothetical extraterrestrial civilization behaves like
  >Europeans or Pacific Islanders (or any number of nonhuman
  >species that have a pattern of expanding into new territory),
  >and has access to technology on par with advanced nuclear
  >rocketry (plus self-contained biospheres, good shielding and
  >other technicalities). It is a conservative model, and it says

  From: Ray Dickenso <ray.dickenson.nul>

  Subject: Some Fell On Stony Ground

  Just now we're becoming aware that most building blocks of life
  are being made in deep space - but not on rocky planets:
  http://web99.arc.nasa.gov/~astrochm/compare.html
  [Earth is a "rocky" planet and they're smallish - but maybe half
  of planets seem to be gas giants, with extremes of temperature
  and sometimes complicated chemical atmospheres]
  Molecular clouds in deep space are building compounds at least
  all the way to amino acids - one step from proteins, and they're
  just one step from "life":
  http://loke.as.arizona.edu/~ckulesa/research/overview.html
  quote - "it appears that the most fundamental physical processes
  that serve as necessary conditions for the formation of life on
  Earth appear to happen elsewhere, and maybe everywhere."
  It also seems that Fred Hoyle was right: life on Earth was
  hastened, maybe directly engendered, by deposition - from space
  - of the necessary building blocks, perhaps proteins and even
  more (we haven't looked into most of deep space yet).
  So there's a strong possibility that organic life - in our
  likeness - is on all suitable rocky planets.
  But what about the "seeds of life" that fell elsewhere?
  Seems to me there's at least two (maybe more) possibilities - a)
  organic life arising in or below the complex atmospheres of gas
  giants;
  b) organic life arising directly in those molecular clouds -
  remember Fred Hoyle's sci-fi novel "The Black Cloud"?
  [And of course there's an even faster route to life - direct
  energy patterns (check friend-foe.txt). They could've been
  around from the start; that's a fourteen billion years lead on
  us.]

  Cheers
  Ray D
  BTW - good review of the processes involved, in "Stardust:
  Supernovae and Life - The Cosmic Connection" by John Gribbin,
  Mary Gribbin.

                                   A mailing list for the study of UFO-related phenomena
