  Listarians -
  Interesting article over at Philip Coppens' site about Los Alamos
  chemist Leon Davidson's attempt to debunk saucers. But not as swamp
  gas - rather, he blamed them largely on the good old CIA!
  Coppens quotes him as saying:
  "It became clear [to me], early in the 1950's, that the CIA,
  specifically Allen Dulles, had used legitimate 'flying saucers'
  events
  <snip>
  as a tool in the Cold War.
  Dulles wanted Russia to waste effort on defences against objects
  having the extreme capabilities implied by the public saucer
  stories.
  Dulles also adopted a concept from his old friend Carl Jung, and
  co-opted the myth that benign aliens have visited Earth for
  millennia. He used magician's illusions, tricks, and showmanship to
  blend in sightings, landings, and contacts, with the legitimate
  military test sightings. The public perception grew (from comic
  book to TV show) that space travel was a real possibility, easing
  Congressional appropriations for the 'moon race' with Russia.
  Later, Dulles found the saucer believers and their clubs an ideal
  propaganda vehicle."

  Now, I've never heard of Davidson before, and though I have no
  doubt that Spookmaster Supreme Dulles would have been delighted to
  pull the wool over the Reds' eyes any way he could, this does not
  make much sense to me.
  Even if the weapons would be useless against "real" UFOs (a dubious
  proposition also), why inspire our enemies to try to develop
  devices that might not be so ineffective against our own advanced
  aircraft? This seems about as silly as the idea that the real
  purpose of Star Wars program was to cause the Russians to give up
  in despair...
  Davidson also fingered Adamski as a government disinfo agent. With
  that I quite agree, as the myth of the Space Brothers would be just
  the thing to calm everything down. But sadly, this whole effort
  seems to me to be just another layer of smoke over Roswell.
  http://www.philipcoppens.com/davidson.html
  (Coppens also has several articles of interest to the List on
  remote viewing and the Nine, but that's worthy of another time...)

  Keep watching the skies!
  Jay Nelson
  http://www.weirdload.com

  Some Comments:
  When someone claims that they can do something, it is up to them to
  show that it is so. It really is as simple as that. You say you can
  do something? Then, prove it, and show your work. Anecdotal
  evidence is not sufficient. So far, none of the methodologically
  sound studies have shown that voice stress analysis techniques (any
  of them) are any better than chance. Bottom line? If you're guilty,
  then you're better off taking the test, because you have about a
  50% chance of "passing" and then the cops might go away and leave
  you alone. But if you're not guilty, then you should definitely not
  take the test, since you also have about a 50% chance of "failing"
  the test.
  There is also a serious ethical issue: Part of the method, for both
  conventional polygraph and VSA involves attempts to convince the
  subject that if they lie they will get caught. Various statements
  are made about microtremors and the machines to analyze them. Yet,
  they can't prove these claims. While it might not be "illegal" to
  make such claims, it certainly looks unethical.

  Posted by: Randy at July 15, 2005 11:55 AM
  I happen to be a CVSA Examiner. I have performed over 500
  examinations in the past 6 years, most of them pre-employment
  examinations for law enforcement agencies.
  Much of the bad info comes from the pro-polygraph folks who see
  their employment base erroding.
  Let me give easy success examples. In pre employment exams, we ask
  about criminal behavior or past uncaught criminal behavior. One
  area we query is sexual crimes. The actual CVSA examinaton comes
  after an extensive interview. Now, most people have not committed a
  sexual crime (rape, forced oral copulation, etc). Occasionally
  you'll find those who have used a prostitute, which may be legal or
  illegal, depending on the location, but in any case, normal
  prostitution is, at most, a misdemeanor. Anyway, people will
  frequently hit or show deception on that question. Upon asking
  further, I'll find that they cheated in a relationship or were
  involved with someone married, had pre-marital sex or something
  similar. Not a crime, but enough that they think about this and it
  causes a reaction. Once we have covered this issue and the question
  is reasked stating we are not talking about this issue, they will
  clear the question with no deception indicated. Some may ask why we
  don't cover the 'cheating' type issues in advance? Our goal is to
  get them to pass and we are not going to broach into those areas
  unless we must. One more important item. The instrument doesn't
  operate itself or draw its own conclusions. You must be a trained
  examiner, just as you must be to perform the polygraph.

  >Interesting article over at Philip Coppens' site about Los Alamos
  chemist Leon Davidson's attempt to debunk saucers. But not as swamp
  gas - rather, he blamed them largely on the good old CIA!
  >Coppens quotes him as saying:
  >"It became clear [to me], early in the 1950's, that the CIA,
  specifically Allen Dulles, had used legitimate 'flying saucers'
  events as a tool in the Cold War.
  Davidson was well known to anyone who read UFO literature in the
  1950s and '60s. He wrote, for example, for Jim Moseley's Saucer
  News. Davidson had been a scientist at Los Alamos during the green-
  fireball episode and belonged to an informal group of colleagues
  interested in the reports. His most lasting contribution to ufology
  was his publication and circulation of Blue Book Special Report No.
  14. He was the first to note the discrepancy between the report's
  content (effectively pro- UFO) and its summary (the usual Blue Book
  burbling).
  Early on, he came to the belief that saucers were secret earthly
  aircraft whose existence their builders, U.S. agencies, were trying
  to keep secret by, among other things, encouraging a focus on alien
  visitors. He wrote a number of speculative pieces - he had nothing
  in the nature of actual evidence - on the subject, contending in
  one that CIA agents set up Adamski (a notion later picked up, at
  least in general outline, by Jacques Vallee in his 1979 book
  Messengers of Deception). Davidson also thought that the famous
  insignia on Lonnie Zamora's UFO could be rearranged to read "CIA."

  Jerry Clark

  Ed and Listfolk:
  >The only study that was described in any detail was the following:
  >"Using a mock theft scenario, 109 subjects were randomly assigned
  >to two groups and given detection of deception examinations
  >using a CVSA instrument. Subjects on one group were programmed
  >deceptive and participated in taking $100.00 from a metal box
  >located in a scenario room. The non-deceptive group did not
  >participate in the scenarios nor did they have knowledge of the
  >mock theft."
  >The results of this particular study are criticized by those who
  >support the use of the CVSA stating a premise that the CVSA is a
  >stress analyzer that captures and displays degrees of stress based
  >on "jeopardy" and a reasonable degree of accuracy cannot be
  >expected where "jeopardy" does not exist."
  I think the problem is in defining "stress" and "jeopardy," which
  can arise from a variety of causes, as can their absence. I don't
  see any scientific basis to any of this, though I can understand
  how cops could use it to coerce confessions from suspects by
  telling them that they have an ironclad deceit detector at hand.
  That, I would venture, may be how stress detectors are ordinarily
  used.
  It may work as that kind of tool - as a bluff instrument, so to
  speak - but beyond that, it has no demonstrated scientific
  credibility that anybody, including you, has been able to
  demonstrate. Anecdotes about Aristotle Onassis (!) and your
  fishing buddy don't count, I'm afraid.
  The simple truth is that scientists are looking for one thing,
  police investigators another. Ufologists already have enough
  problems with their own credibility without tying themselves to
  dubious "truth" devices. Waving voice-stress analysis to validate
  UFO-related claims is simply to invite fresh bouts of ridicule, in
  this instance surely deserved. Thanks, but no thanks.

  Jerry Clark

  >safest means of travel. Those at Roswell in 1947 would have
  >transported the stuff in aircraft. They had lots of them and
  >they even had cargo planes to carry lots of stuff. No real
  >reason for an over the road convoy.)
  >That, to me, is some evidence that the event didn't happen. But,
  >it is not my responsibility to prove this didn't happen, but the
  >responsibility of those making the claims to present some
  >evidence it did. That simply hasn't happened yet.
  As another aside can I ask why you carried sensitive munitions by
  convoy when, as you state, they had cargo planes to fly all that sort
  of stuff about? Maybe you can answer and it may give us a clue why
  convoys are sometimes used rather than planes.

  William

Re: Colonel Corso & His Critics - Shell




                                                          UFO Updates
                                     A mailing list for the study of UFO-related phenomena
                                                 'Its All Here In Black & White'
    Location: UFOUpDatesList.Com > 2006 > Jan > Jan 30

                                                Re: Colonel Corso & His Critics - Shell
  From: Bob Shell <bob.nul>
  Date: Mon, 30 Jan 2006 08:24:10 -0500
  Fwd Date: Mon, 30 Jan 2006 08:49:12 -0500
  Subject: Re: Colonel Corso & His Critics - Shell

  >From: Robert Gates <RGates8254.nul>
  >To: ufoupdates.nul
  >Date: Sun, 29 Jan 2006 19:26:34 EST
  >Subject: Re: Colonel Corso & His Critics
  >So you have Birnes indicating that he faithfully recorded
  >everything correctly as Corso told the story and you have Corso
  >himself indicating that the book was not correct - supposedly
  >because he never had a chance to review the manuscript before
  >publication.
  It is important not to be naive about publishers. I have written
  more than 25 books so far for a number of publishers, and in the
  course of that have encountered exactly one publisher who gives a
  damn whether a book is accurate or not. Most will claim they care,
  but their actions speak louder than their words when they don't fix
  mistakes brought to their attention in plenty of time. One
  publisher of "non-fiction" books told me flat out that he didn't
  care a bit if a book was accurate so long as it sold.
  In the case of Beyond Roswell, which I worked on with Philip Mantle
  and Mike Hesemann, I was given proofs of the books and asked to
  fact check them. I created a lengthy list of errors and submitted
  it to the publisher as requested. I was promised that the errors
  would be fixed. I was outraged when I got my copies of the final
  book and found that not a single one of my corrections had been
  made! I was then told that the corrections would be made in
  subsequent printings and on the CD ROM version. Once again the
  corrections were not made. Many of the criticisms of that book are
  about things that I had pointed out and should have been corrected.
  My point is that it is entirely possible that Corso did review the
  manuscript and make corrections. The publisher would most likely
  have simply ignored them. It costs money to fix things. Most
  publishers will not spend a penny unless forced to.

  Bob Shell

  From: Kevin Randle <KRandle993.nul>
  Date: Mon, 30 Jan 2006 08:40:57 EST
  Fwd Date: Mon, 30 Jan 2006 08:51:58 -0500
  Subject: Re: Why Convoy When You Can Fly? - Randle

  >From: William Sawers <ufsyntax.nul>
  >To: <ufoupdates.nul>
  >Date: Mon, 30 Jan 2006 16:40:19 +1000
  >Subject: Why Convoy When You Can Fly? [was: Colonel Corso & His Critics]

  >>To: ufoupdates.nul
  >>Date: Tue, 24 Jan 2006 11:54:27 EST
  >>Subject: Re: Colonel Corso & His Critics
  >>(As an aside, I spent time in an aviation unit and we used those
  >>assets just as we all use our cars. If we needed to go
  >>somewhere, we used a helicopter because it was the fastest and
  >>safest means of travel. Those at Roswell in 1947 would have
  >>transported the stuff in aircraft. They had lots of them and
  >>they even had cargo planes to carry lots of stuff. No real
  >>reason for an over the road convoy.)
  >>That, to me, is some evidence that the event didn't happen. But,
  >>it is not my responsibility to prove this didn't happen, but the
  >>responsibility of those making the claims to present some
  >>evidence it did. That simply hasn't happened yet.
  >As another aside can I ask why you carried sensitive munitions by
  >convoy when, as you state, they had cargo planes to fly all that sort
  >of stuff about? Maybe you can answer and it may give us a clue why
  >convoys are sometimes used rather than planes.

  >William
  Good Morning, William, List, All -
  Sure. When we moved our weapons we were not an aviation unit, but a
  ground-based Signal Battalion. We did not have easy access to the
  aviation assets. My point was that the aviation units tended to
  think in terms of aviation, especially when they 'owned' the
  assets. The best way available to the 509th Bomb Group with its
  cargo planes was to move the stuff by air. It limited the time
  needed to get the stuff to Wright Field, eliminated the need for
  stops at other locations, and reduced the possibility for
  contamination by Officers and NCOs who would violate regulations.
  There are lots of things that move in convoys... and once we had
  arrived at Ft. Riley, we loaded all that ground equipment,
  something like 550 pieces of rolling stock on railway cars to be
  sent to port to be shipped into the Middle East. Then, we moved the
  weapons, and the soldiers, by air.
  So, the answer is really a matter of what is available, what needs
  to be moved, and how many soldiers are available to move it.

  KRandle
